title: L. LLM Training
statement:
You are given a text dataset. Your task is to train LLM (Large Language Model) and find the minimal possible loss. No kidding.

A text dataset is an array of texts t_1, t_2, …, t_n. Each text t_i is a sequence of tokens. We define the set of tokens T as the set of all tokens that appear in at least one text t_i. Additionally, for each text t_i, there is a set of positions L_i ⊆ {1, 2, …, |t_i|}. The token t_i[j] is generated by LLM if j ∈ L_i and is written by the user if j ∉ L_i.

Let us define LLM with context size k as a probabilistic model P_k, such that it defines the probability distribution of the next token of the sequence, depending on a context w — a sequence of length between 0 and k (inclusive) whose elements are from T. Thus the probabilistic model P_k is a large table of probabilities P_k(next | w), defined for any context w ∈ T^{*}, 0 ≤ |w| ≤ k and any token next ∈ T. Conditions 0 ≤ P_k(next | w) ≤ 1 and ∑limits_{next ∈ T} P_k(next | w) = 1 should be satisfied.

The loss function of LLM with the context size k is the following function defined for P_k:

mathcalL_k(P_k) ,, = ,, ∑_{i=1}^n ,, ∑_{j∈ L_i} , -log_2 P_k!left( underbracet_i[j]_{next token} middle| underbracet_i[max(1,j-k),..,j-1]_context right)

Here t_i[l,..,r] = t_i[l] t_i[l+1] … t_i[r] is the substring from l-th to r-th token, t_i[1,..,0] is an empty string. So, for each text and for each token that is generated by LLM, we add to the loss the negative logarithm (base 2) of the probability that this token will be generated, depending on the substring of previous k tokens (or the whole prefix, if it has length less than k). If the probability is zero, we assume that the negative logarithm is +∞. This loss function is known as the (base 2) Cross Entropy Loss over the LLM-generated positions. The smaller the loss function value mathcalL_k(P_k), the better LLM P_k is.

For each 0 ≤ k < maxlimits_{i=1..n} |t_i|, calculate the minimum possible loss mathcalL_k(P_k) that could be obtained for some P_k — LLM with context size k. It can be proved that this minimum is reachable and is not infinite.

The first line contains a single integer n (1 ≤ n ≤ 10^5) — the number of texts in the dataset. Text descriptions follow.

The first line of the i-th text description contains a single integer m_i (1 ≤ m_i ≤ 3·10^5) — the length of t_i (m_i = |t_i|).

The next line contains m_i strings t_i[1], t_i[2], …, t_i[m_i] (1 ≤ |t_i[j]| ≤ 5) — tokens of the text t_i. Each token consists of symbols with ASCII codes from 33 to 126 (printable characters).

The next line contains a string ell_i of m_i letters U and L, which encodes the set L_i. All positions with the letter L are generated by LLM, and all positions with the letter U are written by the user. So L_i = {j,|,ell_i[j] = textttL}. It is guaranteed that the last token is generated by LLM, so ell_i[m_i] = textttL.

It is guaranteed that the sum of m_i for all i (1 ≤ i ≤ n) does not exceed 3·10^5.

Print M = maxlimits_{i=1..n} m_i real numbers: for each k = 0, 1, …, M-1 print the minimum possible loss mathcalL_k(P_k) for all possible P_k — LLM with context size k.

Your answers will be accepted if their absolute or relative errors do not exceed 10^{-6}; formally, if p is your answer, and q is the jury's answer, this should hold: (|p - q|)/(max{1, |q|}) ≤ 10^{-6}.
